check:
echo "lkme-check 1"
echo "system $(uname -sm)$(grep -qi microsoft /proc/version 2>/dev/null && echo ' WSL')"
docker info --format 'docker {{.ServerVersion}} memory {{.MemTotal}}' 2>/dev/null | grep '^docker [0-9]' || echo "docker not-running"
command -v kubectl >/dev/null && kubectl version --client 2>/dev/null | sed -n 's/^Client Version: /kubectl /p' || echo "kubectl missing"
command -v k3d >/dev/null && k3d version 2>/dev/null | sed -n 's/^k3d version /k3d /p' || echo "k3d missing"
command -v aws >/dev/null && echo "aws $(aws --version 2>&1 | cut -d' ' -f1)" || echo "aws missing"
aws sts get-caller-identity >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "aws-signed-in yes" || echo "aws-signed-in no"
command -v eksctl >/dev/null && echo "eksctl $(eksctl version 2>/dev/null)" || echo "eksctl missing"

requirements.intro: Check these before you install anything. They match the first step of the start guide.

items.label: Memory
items.text: 8 GB of RAM or more. Docker gets half of it by default, and 4 GB is enough for the dashboard and a practice cluster.

systems.macos: macOS, a version Docker Desktop supports: the current release or one of the two before it.
systems.windows: Windows 10 22H2 or Windows 11 23H2 or later, Pro, Enterprise, or Education, with WSL 2.

items.label: Internet
items.text: A steady connection. The practice cluster downloads Kubernetes the first time.

items.label: Permission to install apps
items.text: On a work laptop you may need help from your IT team.

items.label: For Lab 2 and EKS only lessons
items.text: An AWS account. AWS charges for the cluster while it runs.

installScript.title: Install everything with one script
installScript.text: The script prints what it finds about your laptop, installs only what is missing, then runs the check in step 4 for you. It is safe to run again. Download it, open it to read it if you like, then run it. It asks for your password when it installs something.

macos.expect: It installs Git, Docker Desktop, kubectl, k3d, the AWS CLI, and eksctl, and ends with the check's output between two dashed lines. Paste those lines into step 5. When Docker Desktop first starts, read its agreement and select Accept.

windows.where: Open PowerShell as administrator: click Start, type PowerShell, right-click Windows PowerShell, and select Run as administrator. Then run these. -ExecutionPolicy Bypass lets this one PowerShell run the script you downloaded, without changing your laptop's settings.
windows.expect: The first run installs Git, Docker Desktop, and Ubuntu on WSL 2. It may then ask you to restart and to open Ubuntu once to choose a user name and password, and it tells you what to run next. The next run installs kubectl, k3d, the AWS CLI, and eksctl inside Ubuntu, and ends with the check's output between two dashed lines. Paste those lines into step 5.

linux.where: For Ubuntu and Debian. Run these in Terminal as yourself, not as root.
linux.expect: It installs Docker Engine, Git, kubectl, k3d, the AWS CLI, and eksctl, and ends with the check's output between two dashed lines. Paste those lines into step 5. If it added you to the docker group, log out and back in before you use docker in a new terminal.

steps.text: Open PowerShell as administrator and run this. It installs Ubuntu, and WSL too if Docker Desktop hasn't. Restart when it asks, then Ubuntu asks you to choose a user name and password.
In Docker Desktop, open Settings, then Resources, then WSL integration. Turn on Ubuntu and select Apply & restart.
Open Ubuntu from the Start menu. Run every command on this page, and every lab command, in Ubuntu.

tools.name: Docker
tools.what: Runs the dashboard, and the practice cluster for Lab 1.

macos.text: You already have Docker Desktop, because the dashboard runs in it. Start it before Lab 1.

windows.text: You already have Docker Desktop, because the dashboard runs in it. Turn on its WSL integration for Ubuntu, as the first card says.

linux.text: You already have Docker, because the dashboard runs in it. Start it before Lab 1, and check that docker info works without sudo.

tools.name: kubectl
tools.what: The command you use to talk to a cluster.

macos.text: Install it with Homebrew. If brew --version doesn't work, first install Homebrew with the command on brew.sh.

windows.text: In Ubuntu, download kubectl 1.37.2, check the download, and install it. On an ARM64 laptop, replace amd64 with arm64.
windows.commands:
curl -LO "https://dl.k8s.io/release/v1.37.2/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl"
curl -LO "https://dl.k8s.io/release/v1.37.2/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl.sha256"
echo "$(cat kubectl.sha256)  kubectl" | sha256sum --check
sudo install -o root -g root -m 0755 kubectl /usr/local/bin/kubectl

linux.text: Download kubectl 1.37.2, check the download, and install it. On an ARM64 machine, replace amd64 with arm64.
linux.commands:
curl -LO "https://dl.k8s.io/release/v1.37.2/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl"
curl -LO "https://dl.k8s.io/release/v1.37.2/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl.sha256"
echo "$(cat kubectl.sha256)  kubectl" | sha256sum --check
sudo install -o root -g root -m 0755 kubectl /usr/local/bin/kubectl

tools.what: Creates a small practice cluster inside Docker.

windows.text: In Ubuntu, download the official installer, read it, then run it.

linux.text: Download the official installer, read it, then run it.

tools.what: Lets your terminal use your AWS account.

macos.text: Download the official installer and run it.

windows.text: In Ubuntu, download and install it. On an ARM64 laptop, replace x86_64 with aarch64. If unzip is missing, run sudo apt install unzip first.

linux.text: Download and install it. On an ARM64 machine, replace x86_64 with aarch64.

tools.after: Then sign in with aws configure, or aws sso login if your company uses IAM Identity Center.

tools.name: eksctl
tools.what: Creates and deletes the EKS cluster for Lab 2.

macos.text: Install it from the AWS Homebrew tap.
macos.commands:
brew tap aws/tap
brew install aws/tap/eksctl

windows.text: In Ubuntu, download the latest release and install it. On an ARM64 laptop, set ARCH=arm64.
windows.commands:
ARCH=amd64
PLATFORM=$(uname -s)_$ARCH
curl -sLO "https://github.com/eksctl-io/eksctl/releases/latest/download/eksctl_$PLATFORM.tar.gz"
tar -xzf eksctl_$PLATFORM.tar.gz -C /tmp && rm eksctl_$PLATFORM.tar.gz
sudo install -m 0755 /tmp/eksctl /usr/local/bin && rm /tmp/eksctl

linux.text: Download the latest release and install it. On an ARM64 machine, set ARCH=arm64.
linux.commands:
ARCH=amd64
PLATFORM=$(uname -s)_$ARCH
curl -sLO "https://github.com/eksctl-io/eksctl/releases/latest/download/eksctl_$PLATFORM.tar.gz"
tar -xzf eksctl_$PLATFORM.tar.gz -C /tmp && rm eksctl_$PLATFORM.tar.gz
sudo install -m 0755 /tmp/eksctl /usr/local/bin && rm /tmp/eksctl

practiceCluster.intro: Anywhere lessons run their Try it commands on a free practice cluster called practice. kubectl can know several clusters, such as an EKS cluster from Lab 2. It sends every command to the one you chose last, so you choose the practice cluster before you practise.

steps.title: Do this once: create the practice cluster
steps.text: Docker must be running. This creates the cluster in about a minute, points kubectl at it, and lists its node.
steps.commands:
k3d cluster create practice --image rancher/k3s:v1.37.2-k3s1 --wait
kubectl config use-context k3d-practice
kubectl get nodes
steps.expect: Cluster 'practice' created successfully, then Switched to context "k3d-practice", then one node named k3d-practice-server-0 with STATUS Ready.

steps.title: Every time you practise: point kubectl at it
steps.text: Start Docker Desktop first. Then run these two lines before your first Try it, even if you ran them yesterday. Lab 1, Lab 2, and EKS only lessons point kubectl at other clusters.
steps.commands:
kubectl config use-context k3d-practice
kubectl get nodes
steps.expect: Switched to context "k3d-practice", then the node with STATUS Ready. Now every Try it command goes to your practice cluster.

sources.title: Organizing cluster access using kubeconfig files

problems.message: error: no context exists with the name: "k3d-practice"
problems.text: kubectl doesn't know the practice cluster. If the first line lists practice, the second adds it back. If not, use the Do this once card.
problems.commands:
k3d cluster list
k3d kubeconfig merge practice --kubeconfig-merge-default --kubeconfig-switch-context

problems.message: The connection to the server ... was refused
problems.text: Run the every-time card first. If you still see this, the practice cluster isn't running. Start Docker Desktop, then start the cluster.

problems.message: the server could not find the requested resource
problems.text: kubectl isn't pointing at any cluster, so it reached the dashboard at localhost:8080. Point it at the practice cluster.

problems.message: Failed to create cluster 'practice' because a cluster with that name already exists
problems.text: You created it before, so there is nothing to fix. Run the every-time card.

insideNode.intro: Optional. Do it now, or come back after your first lessons. Your practice cluster's node is a Docker container, so it has no SSH. docker exec opens a shell inside it instead, the way SSH opens one on a server. Then you can see where Kubernetes keeps its parts. On EKS Auto Mode, AWS runs the API server and etcd and the nodes allow no SSH, so your practice cluster is the place to see them.
insideNode.warning: Look, don't change. Inside the node you are root, so nothing stops you. Don't edit, move, or delete anything you see there: K3s uses these files while it runs, and one change can break your practice cluster. Never print or share the token in /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/token or any .key file. Anyone who has them controls your cluster.

steps.title: Open a shell on the node
steps.text: Your practice cluster has one node, the Docker container k3d-practice-server-0. This runs a shell inside it.
steps.expect: The prompt changes to ~ #. The # means you are root, inside the node, and the next commands run there.

steps.title: See the control plane run
steps.text: The control plane is the API server, the scheduler, the controller manager, and the datastore. A kubeadm cluster runs each part as its own Pod, from a file in /etc/kubernetes/manifests. K3s runs them all inside one k3s server process.
steps.expect: /bin/k3s server, and containerd, which runs the containers. No kube-apiserver, kube-scheduler, or kube-controller-manager process appears.

steps.title: Where every object is stored
steps.text: Everything you apply, from Pods to Secrets, is saved here. Most clusters use etcd for this. K3s uses a SQLite database by default.
steps.expect: state.db, the database, and two working files next to it.

steps.title: Certificates and keys
steps.text: The parts of the cluster prove who they are to each other with these certificates. A kubeadm cluster keeps them in /etc/kubernetes/pki.
steps.expect: .crt and .key files for each part, such as client-admin.crt and client-scheduler.key.

steps.title: Files K3s applies by itself
steps.text: K3s applies the files here like kubectl apply, and writes its own again each time it starts. That is how CoreDNS and metrics-server got into your cluster.
steps.expect: coredns.yaml, local-storage.yaml, traefik.yaml, and a metrics-server folder, with a few more.

steps.title: The containers on this node
steps.text: kubectl asks the API server about Pods. crictl asks containerd on this node about the containers that make them up.
steps.expect: One row for each running container, with its POD and NAMESPACE, such as coredns in kube-system.

steps.title: Container logs
steps.text: Each container writes its log to a file on its node. When you run kubectl logs, the kubelet reads these files.
steps.expect: One folder for each Pod, named after its namespace, Pod name, and ID, such as kube-system_coredns-...

steps.title: Leave the node
steps.text: This closes the shell. The node and your cluster keep running.
steps.expect: Your laptop's own prompt comes back. Docker Desktop may also print a What's next tip about docker debug. You don't need it.

startAgain.text: Changed or deleted something by mistake? Delete the practice cluster, then run the Do this once card in step 6 again. You lose only what you applied to the cluster. Your lesson files stay on your laptop.
